summary: Swiss food giant Nestlé pushed infant formula on poor mothers in the developing world from the 1960s with fake nurses, free hospital samples and fear-based ads; unsafe water and over-dilution left vast numbers of babies malnourished or dead.
keywords: International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes

evidence.note: covered_span start: ~6 min on Henri Nestlé's 1867 formula; host says the founder was not the bastard
1930s doctor links formula to malnutrition; company starts selling formula as better than breast milk
Abbott designs maternity wards and funds doctors to steer mothers to bottle feeding
1960s-70s push into the global South begins; uniformed mothercraft nurses sent into hospitals
sales tactics around hospital bans in Singapore, Jamaica and the Philippines
fear-based ad campaigns (Lactogen, a Congo radio jingle) and War on Want's critique of them
rural Nigeria study finds almost no mothers actually unable to breastfeed
1950s Cooperstown studies and later data on illness and malnutrition in formula-fed infants
Jamaican case of starving babies on diluted formula, told to a US Senate subcommittee
1981 WHO marketing code; a decade later (1991) the Ivory Coast case shows marketing continued
Ivorian authorities restrict free samples and Nestlé cuts off formula to hospitals
2018 WHA breastfeeding resolution fight and 2018 Changing Markets report: issue ongoing

notes: main_span 1960-1991: developing-world marketing to the 1991 Ivory Coast case; covered_span 1867-2018 adds Henri Nestlé (~6 min) and the 2018 segment. Wet-nursing history is background. Setting lists harm countries first; CH dropped. medical-malpractice: ~8 min (00:21-00:29) on co-opted hospitals and doctors. Enslaved wet nurses (~2 min) too short for slavery theme/warning. child-death for starving-infant accounts at ~00:49 and ~00:53.
